bylines.bio: Mara edits the journal and keeps the studio's style guide honest. She has spent fifteen years making software documentation feel less like a manual and more like a place.
Theo builds the tools the studio writes with. He is interested in small systems, long-lived files, and interfaces that explain themselves.
Inês is a designer and letterpress printer. She writes about place, typography, and the relationship between a map and the ground it describes.

data.title: Contact
data.excerpt: Write to the studio about editorial work, design systems, or a project that needs a second reader.

children.text: We read everything that arrives, but we answer slowly. A useful note tells us what you are making, who it is for, and what kind of help you need.
What to expect
Most replies go out within a week. If your note is about a workshop or a speaking invitation, include the date and the audience, and we will tell you honestly whether it fits.

data.title: Getting started
data.summary: How the Fieldwork handbook is organised, and how to add a chapter without inventing a new process.

children.text: The handbook is the internal counterpart to the journal. It holds the practices we want to repeat, not the announcements we want people to read.
How a chapter is structured
Every chapter uses the same contract: a title, a one-sentence summary, a section, an order, and a last-updated date. Everything else is written in the body.
The
section
groups related chapters in the index. The order controls their position inside that group.
If you are unsure where a chapter belongs, start with the section that already contains the closest neighbour. A new section is a bigger decision than a new chapter.

data.title: Writing style
data.summary: The small rules that keep our voice consistent without making every piece sound the same.

children.text: We write to be understood on the first read and remembered on the second. That means short sentences, concrete nouns, and a willingness to cut the sentence that only exists to introduce the next one.
Rules we actually use
Prefer the concrete verb to the abstract noun.
Read the piece aloud before it goes to review.
If a paragraph needs a diagram to make sense, it needs another draft first.
What we avoid
We avoid urgency language, invented categories, and the assumption that the reader has been following along. Every piece should stand on its own.

data.title: Editorial workflow
data.summary: From pitch to publish: the five states every Fieldwork piece passes through.

children.text: A piece moves through five states. The names matter less than the fact that everyone can see which state a draft is in.
The five states
Pitch: one paragraph and a reason to write it now.
Draft: written for the editor, not the audience.
Review: read aloud, marked up, and returned with questions.
Proof: a final pass for links, names, and dates.
Publish: scheduled, announced, and added to the next reading list.
A piece can move backwards. A proof that turns up a structural problem goes back to review, and the calendar moves with it.

data.title: Publishing checklist
data.summary: The last twenty minutes before a piece goes live.

children.text: The checklist is deliberately short. If it takes longer than twenty minutes, something earlier in the process was skipped.
Before you press publish
Read the title and excerpt as a pair, not separately.
Check every link, including the ones you added yesterday.
Confirm the byline, category, and tags.
Look at the page on a narrow screen.
Schedule the newsletter note for the same morning.

data.title: Keeping field notes
data.summary: How we collect observations so that a place, a conversation, or a detail can survive until the first draft.

children.text: A field note is not a draft. It is a record of attention: what was there, what was said, and what you almost missed.
What to write down
Write the exact words people use, the names of things, and the small physical details that make a scene legible later. Leave the interpretation for the draft.
The notebook is not where you decide what a thing means. It is where you keep enough of the thing that you can decide later.

data.title: A manifesto for fieldwork
data.excerpt: Why we write from a place instead of a platform, and what a small editorial studio can still promise.

children.text: Fieldwork began as a shared notebook. Three people, a table by a window, and a rule that anything worth publishing was worth reading aloud first.
The notebook became a journal, the journal became a practice, and the practice is still the same: pay attention, write it down, and edit until the reader can see what you saw.
What we mean by fieldwork

Fieldwork is the part of the work that happens before the work: the walk, the interview, the half-hour spent watching someone use the thing you built. It is not research in the formal sense. It is attention with a notebook.
The opposite of a platform is not a smaller platform. It is a place with a door and a person who answers it.
A small set of commitments
Publish less, and read it more than once.
Keep the tools legible enough that the team can maintain them.
Write the handbook before the process drifts.
The longer version of these commitments lives in the
handbook
. It is the internal counterpart to this journal, and the place we revise first.

data.title: The case for slow software
data.excerpt: Fast software optimises the moment. Slow software respects the afternoon. A note on building for the second read.

children.text: There is a kind of software that treats every second of the user's attention as a resource to be captured. It is very good at what it does. It is also exhausting to live inside.
The cost of always-on
When every surface is optimised for the next click, the user never gets to finish a thought. The interface is not slow because it is badly built. It is slow because it keeps interrupting.
Slow software makes a different bet: that a person who is allowed to concentrate will come back, and that the relationship is worth more than the session.
Designing for the second read
A page that rewards a second read is not necessarily quieter. It is more legible. The hierarchy holds, the language is specific, and nothing moves unless it has a reason to.
Speed is a feature. Calm is a property of the whole system, and it is much harder to add later.
We are not arguing for sluggishness. We are arguing for a pace that leaves room for the reader to arrive. That is a design decision, and it belongs in the brief.

data.title: Designing for the second read
data.excerpt: The first read is for orientation. The second is where a piece of writing, or an interface, earns its place.

children.text: Most design decisions are made for the first read: the glance, the scroll, the five-second test. That is a reasonable place to start. It is a poor place to stop.
Attention is the interface
A second read happens when the reader trusts the page enough to slow down. Trust is built by consistency: the same heading sizes, the same link treatment, the same promise about what a click will do.
Inconsistency is expensive in a quiet way. Every small surprise asks the reader to re-orient, and re-orientation is the opposite of reading.
Three small tests
Read the page without clicking anything. Is the argument still clear?
Cover the navigation. Does the content still tell you where you are?
Read it on a narrow screen. Did anything important disappear?
None of these tests require a prototype. They require a page that is willing to be read, which is mostly a matter of restraint.

data.title: A small CMS for a small team
data.excerpt: Why we moved our editorial workflow into a content model designed for three people instead of three hundred.

children.text: Our editorial team is small. For a long time that meant a shared document, a folder of drafts, and a release checklist that lived in someone's head. It worked, mostly, until it did not.
The shape of the content
Fieldwork has four collections. Each one has a route, a set of fields, and a reason to exist that can be explained in one sentence.
Journal: long-form notes, ordered by their own date field.
Handbook: internal practice, grouped by section and order.
Events: readings and workshops, with a real date range.
Pages: standalone pages, built from reusable blocks.
The route comes from the collection. That sounds obvious, but it means a new section is a folder and a schema, not a new application.
A content model is a promise about what the team will be able to change without asking a developer. Keep the promise small enough to keep.

data.title: Notes on printing a place
data.excerpt: A letterpress project about a neighbourhood, and what a map leaves out when it decides what counts as a landmark.

children.text: The project started with a walk and a camera, and ended with a small letterpress book that fits in a coat pocket. It is not a guide. It is an argument about what a neighbourhood is made of.
A map is an argument

Every map decides what to include. The official map includes the station, the church, and the supermarket. Our map includes the bench where the same three people eat lunch, the door that is always propped open, and the wall that has been repaired four times.
A place is not a set of coordinates. It is a set of repeated gestures, and the surfaces that remember them.

The printing was deliberately modest: two colours, one typeface, a cover that could take being carried around. The constraints made the editing easier. When you cannot add another spread, you have to decide what the book is actually about.

data.title: The tools we keep
data.excerpt: A short inventory of the software and objects that have survived more than one year in the studio.

children.text: Every year or so we empty the studio's tool shelf and ask the same question: did this earn its place? Most things do not survive the question. The ones that do tend to be small, legible, and a little boring.
Tools that keep
Plain text files, because they outlive the applications that edit them.
A notebook with a sewn binding, because it opens flat.
A publishing workflow that can be explained in a paragraph.
What we retired

The project management tool with fourteen views. The analytics dashboard nobody opened. The custom static site generator that only one person could run. All of them promised leverage and delivered maintenance.
The test is not whether a tool is good. It is whether the team can keep it good without making it the work.
